stem: Use the diagram. Give another name for plane K.
title: Another name for a plane
steps: Plane K contains D, E, F, G, and H.
A plane can be named with one capital letter, like plane K, or with three points that are in it. Plane K contains points D, E, F, G, and H.
J is on line c, above the plane: not in plane K.
Point J is on line c, but it sits above the plane, so we can't use J.
The three points can't all be on one line.
The three points also can't all lie on one line. D, E, and F are all on line k, so don't use those three together.
plane FHG
F, H, and G are in the plane and are not on one line. So another name is plane F H G. Other answers like plane D H G work too.

stem: Use the diagram. Name a point that is not coplanar with E, G, and H.
title: A point that is not coplanar
steps: E, G, and H are in plane L.
Coplanar points lie in the same plane. E, G, and H are all in plane L.
Which point is not in plane L?
So look for a point that is not in plane L.
K is on line j, above the plane.
Point K is on line j, but it is above the plane, not in it. Every other point is in plane L.
K
So the answer is K.

stem: Use the diagram. Give another name for line DH.
title: Another name for a line
steps: Line DH goes through D, E, and H: it is line m.
A line can be named by any two of its points, or by its lowercase letter. D, E, and H are all on line m.
line m, line DE, line EH, line HD, …
So line D H is also line m, line D E, line E H, or line H D. The order of the two points doesn't matter.
line HD
One answer is line H D.

stem: Use the diagram. Name three collinear points.
title: Three collinear points
steps: collinear: on the same line
Collinear points lie on the same line.
K, L, and M are all on line d.
Points K, L, and M are all on line d.
K, L, and M
So K, L, and M are collinear. Watch out: Q is on line w, not line d, so it can't be used with K and M.

stem: Use the diagram. Name the intersection of line k and plane X.
title: The intersection of a line and a plane
steps: Line k crosses plane X.
Line k is not in plane X. It passes through it.
It crosses at point S.
A line that crosses a plane meets it at one point. Line k goes through plane X at point S.
point S
So the intersection is point S.

stem: Use the diagram. What is another name for ray PQ?
title: Another name for a ray
steps: Ray PQ starts at P and goes through Q.
A ray is named by its endpoint first, then any other point on it. Ray P Q starts at P and goes through Q.
It keeps going through R.
It keeps going in the same direction, through R.
ray PR
So ray P Q is also ray P R. The endpoint P always comes first.

stem: Use the diagram. What is another name for Q̅P̅?
title: Another name for a segment
steps: Q̅P̅: the segment with endpoints Q and P
Q P with a bar over it is a segment. Its endpoints are Q and P.
P̅Q̅
A segment can be named with its endpoints in either order. So Q P is also P Q.

stem: Use the diagram. Name a pair of opposite rays.
title: A pair of opposite rays
steps: opposite rays: same endpoint, opposite directions, one line
Opposite rays share an endpoint and point in opposite directions along the same line.
On line u, P is between H and Q.
On line u, point P is between H and Q.
ray PH and ray PQ
So ray P H and ray P Q are opposite rays. Ray P T and ray P S, on line m, are another pair.

stem: Use the diagram. Name all rays with endpoint G.
title: All rays with a given endpoint
steps: G is where lines j and a cross.
Point G is where the two lines cross.
From G, a ray goes toward each other point.
From G, there is one ray toward each point on the lines: F, K, H, and J.
ray GF, ray GK, ray GH, ray GJ
So the rays are G F, G K, G H, and G J. Each name starts with G, the endpoint.

stem: Use the diagram. Name a pair of rays that are not opposite rays.
title: Rays that are not opposite
steps: opposite rays: same endpoint, opposite directions, one line
Opposite rays share an endpoint and point in opposite directions along one line.
Pick two rays from L on different lines.
To get rays that are not opposite, pick two rays from L that are on different lines.
ray LH and ray LU
Ray L H is on line m, and ray L U is on line p. They are not opposite rays.

stem: Use the diagram. Name all the points that are not coplanar with points J, H, and L.
title: Points that are not coplanar (box)
steps: J, H, and L are on the bottom face HJKL.
In the box, J, H, and L are corners of the bottom face, H J K L.
K is the fourth corner of that face.
K is the fourth corner of that face, so K is coplanar with them.
The top corners are not in that plane.
The top corners, D, E, F, and G, are not in the plane of the bottom face.
D, E, F, G
So the points that are not coplanar with J, H, and L are D, E, F, and G.

stem: Use the diagram. Name the intersection of plane DHE and plane LQD.
title: The intersection of two planes (box)
steps: Plane DHE is the top face DEHL.
Find the face that holds each plane. D, H, and E are on the top face, D E H L.
Plane LQD is the left face DLXQ.
L, Q, and D are on the left face, D L X Q.
They share edge DL.
Two planes meet in a line. These two faces share the edge D L.
line DL
So the intersection is line D L.

stem: Use the diagram. Name a point that is coplanar with points S, K, and P.
title: A point coplanar with three points (box)
steps: S, K, and P are corners of the face KNSP.
S, K, and P are corners of the left face, K N S P.
The fourth corner is N.
The fourth corner of that face is N.
N
So N is coplanar with S, K, and P.

stem: Name the geometric term modeled by the edge of a ruler.
title: Geometric terms in real life
steps: Point: one location
A point is a single location, like a star in the sky or the tip of a pencil.
Segment: straight, two endpoints
A segment is straight with two endpoints, like the edge of a ruler.
Ray: one endpoint, goes on in one direction
A ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction, like a flashlight beam.
Line: goes on in both directions
A line goes on forever in both directions, like a straight track that never ends.
Plane: a flat surface that goes on forever
A plane is a flat surface, like a floor or a wall that goes on and on.
the edge of a ruler: straight, with two ends → segment
The edge of a ruler is straight and has two ends, so it models a segment.

stem: What is the intersection of a line and a plane, when the line crosses the plane but does not lie in it?
title: What is the intersection?
steps: two lines that cross → a point
Two different lines that cross meet at one point.
two planes that cross → a line
Two different planes that cross meet in a line, like two walls meeting in a corner.
a line crossing a plane → a point
A line that passes through a plane meets it at one point.
a line in a plane → the whole line
If the line lies in the plane, every point of the line is in the plane, so the intersection is the whole line.
parallel planes → no intersection
Parallel planes never meet.
crosses the plane, not in it → a point
In this question, the line crosses the plane but is not in it, so the answer is a point.

stem: 11 points are marked on a line. How many different segments have two of these points as endpoints? How many different rays have one of these points as their endpoint?
title: Challenge: counting segments and rays
steps: 11 points on one line
There are 11 points on a line. Count segments first, then rays.
each point pairs with 10 others: 11 · 10
Every segment uses two of the points. Each point pairs with the 10 others: 11 times 10 is 110.
110 ÷ 2 = 55 segments
That counts every segment twice, once from each end. So divide by 2: 55 segments.
each point: 2 opposite rays → 2 · 11 = 22 rays
Each point is the endpoint of two rays, one going each way. 2 times 11 is 22 rays.
55 segments; 22 rays
So there are 55 segments and 22 rays.
